newsitem.title: USA: Mickey, Hillary mark Disney World's 25th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Mickey, Hillary mark Disney World's 25th birthday.

text.p: Mickey Mouse, who turned central Florida from orange groves and cattle ranches into a fantasy world visited by more than 100 million vacationers, celebrated a 25th anniversary on Tuesday.
The Mouse and thousands of his closest friends gathered at the quarter-century-old Walt Disney World, a playground twice the size of Manhattan that has become an American icon.
First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, Disney chief Michael Eisner, a marching band of 1,076 musicians and a flock of Hollywood stars helped rededicate the Magic Kingdom.

"Thank you for reminding us there are no limits to the American imagination, for encouraging each of us to follow our own dreams and for making children the heart and soul of all your endeavours," Mrs. Clinton said at a carefully scripted ceremony that managed to keep a Florida rain shower in check until the event ended.

Cinderella's Castle, which towers over the Magic Kingdom theme park, was adorned to resemble a 185-foot (55 metre)-tall birthday cake, complete with pink icing and giant candles. Mickey Mouse pranced down Main Street, revelling in his role as master of ceremonies.
Since Disney World opened on Oct. 1, 1971, the Mouse has resculpted much of Central Florida as the world's most popular tourist destination took shape.

The vacation resort has seen explosive growth, evolving from a single theme park and two hotels at the start to today's Epcot Centre, Disney-MGM Studios, two water parks, restaurant and shopping complexes, a town named Celebration, and 15 themed resorts.
And Disney is still building.

A cruise line, a fourth theme park named Animal Kingdom and a major sports complex are among the attractions being developed on top of the company's existing $2 billion investment in Florida. And Disney is trying to stay one step ahead of American trends by developing adult and environmental tourism programmes to keep ageing baby boomers coming back once their children are grown.
"I don't think it can get too big," Eisner told ABC-TV's "Good Morning, America" on Tuesday. "The biggest thing that's wrong is you have to leave."

He also defended the daily cost of admission to the theme parks, which has risen to nearly $42 per adult. "It's much less than even a movie ticket, where you go for two hours," he said, apparently referring to the hourly cost of each type of entertainment.

Mickey Mouse fans would agree, but some old-timers in central Florida blame animator Walt Disney's dream for bringing traffic congestion, runaway suburban growth and seasonal minimum-wage jobs to the region. Disney World also has unique taxing and police powers on its 28,000-acre (11,330 hectares) property.
The imprint of Mickey Mouse, the symbol of Walt Disney World, is everywhere -- in strip shopping centres, T-shirt shops and bumper stickers in Orlando and its suburbs.

"People are very aware of the Orwellian aspect of Disney," one marketing executive from a competing Orlando resort said. She said she worried about the "spreading control" of Disney in central Florida. With the construction of Celebration, Disney now offers people a self-contained city in which to live, complete with a hospital, school and shopping district.
"Disney has a lot of money, and it can do what it damn well pleases," the executive added, speaking on condition of anonymity.

About one in five employees in central Florida work at tourism-related jobs, including the 42,000 "cast members" at Disney World. And Disney's rapid growth has ignited tourism development in cities throughout the state, experts said.

"Disney is attempting to insulate itself from competitors by vertical integration into other industries. For example, Disney is now in lodging in a big way, which allows them to get into conference planning," said Mark Bonn, a professor of marketing at Florida State University's department of hospitality administration. "They've moved backwards and forward to develop new products."

Since Walt Disney World opened its doors in 1971, its guests have included foreign heads of state, U.S. presidents, athletes and movie stars. Although Disney does not release attendance figures, industry analysts estimate that more than 15 million tourists passed through its Florida turnstiles last year.

Disney has devoted new energy and investment to Florida since being rebuffed two years ago by Virginia residents for a proposed American history theme park and having to fight cultural battles with its EuroDisney park in France.

"The world is not always a fair or friendly place," Disney chief Eisner said at the ceremony. "While we can't wave a magic wand and cure the world's ills, we can rededicate ourselves to keep this small corner of the world a place where children will always feel welcome, safe, loved and happy."
